FORGEMCP MILESTONE: END-TO-END PROCEDURAL SKELETAL RIGGING, VERTEX SKINNING & KEYFRAME ANIMATION

From Static 3D Geometry to an Animated Skeletal Hand

Record ID: FMCP-BLENDER-HAND-20261030
Classification: Major technical capability demonstration
Status: FUNCTIONAL PROTOTYPE — ANIMATION CORRECTION REQUIRED
Event date: October 30, 2026
Project: ForgeMCP / Blender
Related records: Incorrect finger flexion direction; proposed anatomical correction milestone; proposed webcam motion-capture milestone.

Executive summary

This milestone records an integrated Blender hand-rigging experiment that moved beyond isolated scene edits. A corrected existing hand mesh was inspected, duplicated into a recoverable rigged copy, given a hand-only bone hierarchy, bound with automatically generated vertex weights, animated through pose-bone channels, and saved as a versioned Blender file. A later read-only ForgeMCP connection opened that saved file and returned matching scene, mesh, armature, skin and Action data. The user also confirmed seeing the hand animate in Blender.

The practical significance is the combination of several operations that character pipelines need to cooperate: geometry and transform inspection, joint placement, skeletal parenting, weight assignment, Armature deformation, keyframe authoring, and result readback. The measured result contains a 22-bone hand skeleton, 21 deform bones, 9,584 mesh vertices, 21,379 weight assignments, and an Action with 57 pose-bone rotation curves and 855 keys over frames 1–120 at 24 frames per second. Isolated deformation tests moved each of the five digit regions while measuring only near-zero average movement in the other digits. The neutral pose is recoverable at frame 120.

This is a functional prototype, not a finished character-rigging product. The user’s visual review identifies the central defect: the fingers bend backward instead of curling toward the palm. Numerical displacement tests establish that the mesh responds to each finger’s pose channels; they do not override the visual finding or prove that the chosen local axes correspond to anatomical flexion. That issue remains open. Full-fist quality, joint paths, mesh intersections, repeated playback in a user-facing review, export, retargeting, and game-engine compatibility have not passed their acceptance gates.

The final v002 artifact uses a custom hand-only armature and native Blender automatic weights. Auto-Rig Pro was installed and its ForgeMCP integration was available, but the delivered v002 rig is not an Auto-Rig Pro rig. The typed ForgeMCP skin-binding preview rejected the source because the mesh’s attribute payload exceeded its configured limit; the successful weighting step ran through Blender’s native automatic-parent operation in a separate Blender process. This distinction matters: ForgeMCP participated in inspection, scene orchestration and readback, while the final weight-generation route was a native Blender operation. The milestone demonstrates an orchestrated workflow, not a universal, one-click ForgeMCP automatic-rigging feature.

Development background and initial challenge

The input was a dense, single-piece mechanical hand mesh in the existing Blender project. The user reported correcting its orientation and transforms, moving its origin near the wrist, removing the previously incorrect skeleton, and clearing obsolete groups and the old Armature modifier before the reconstruction. Those preparation actions are user-confirmed history. In the saved v002 file, the source mesh remains alongside a separate rigged copy, which provides a comparison object and avoids replacing source geometry.

The initial ForgeMCP inspection described the hand as one connected mesh with 9,584 vertices, 28,761 edges and 19,175 polygons. The topology audit reported 43 boundary edges and 86 non-manifold edges; the mesh was not retopologized. Those topology findings are relevant limits for deformation and export review. The weight operation exposed a scale boundary: the source carried 479,365 mesh-attribute entries, above the typed binding preview’s 200,000-entry limit. Auto-Rig Pro’s Match to Rig path also rejected the custom hand armature as not matching an Auto-Rig Pro reference rig. Neither rejection means the mesh could not be weighted; each identifies a boundary in those particular bridge workflows.

The work therefore continued on a separate saved copy with a hand-specific skeleton and Blender’s native automatic weights. No arbitrary-body generalization was inferred from the result.

Evidence and acceptance boundary

This report separates evidence by source:

  • User-confirmed: the source hand was corrected and cleaned before rigging; new bones and weights were created; a hand animation was observed in Blender; the visible fingers bend in the wrong direction.
  • ForgeMCP readback: on October 30, the connected ForgeMCP session reported Blender 5.2.3 LTS, adapter 0.2.49-alpha.1, the v002 file path, five scene objects, frame range 1–120, and 24 fps. Read-only calls inspected the rigged mesh, armature hierarchy, a bounded page of weights and the Action.
  • Saved-file audit: an independent Blender 5.2.3 reopen check measured mesh identity, bone count and parents, weight coverage and normalization, Action channels, key count, individual-digit motion, thumb motion and neutral-pose restoration.
  • Not established: production-quality anatomy, error-free collision, broad topology suitability, all-frame visual quality, export, engine import, retargeting, arbitrary-mesh automation, and webcam tracking.

The readback identified the original mesh as tripo_node_2038746d and the rigged duplicate as tripo_node_2038746d_Rigged. Both have 9,584 vertices, 28,761 edges and 19,175 faces. The rigged copy retained UVMap and material tripo_mat_2038746d; source and copy coordinate and UV deltas were exactly zero in the file audit. Its evaluated neutral-pose delta was approximately 1.33 × 10⁻⁷ Blender units. The rigged mesh object uses location (0, 0, 0), zero rotation and unit scale, and has one visible Armature modifier targeting Hand_Rig_Reconstructed.

Technical capability breakdown

A. Scene and mesh analysis

The bridge’s scene and object inspection tools returned the active Blender file, object types, transforms, mesh counts, materials and modifiers. The rig inspection returned the armature hierarchy and evaluated pose information. The bounded skin inspection returned vertex-to-group weights without changing the scene. Action inspection paged the armature’s F-curves and keyframes.

For this project, scene identity, object identity, mesh counts, transforms, material and UV names, the final modifier target, bone hierarchy, Action name and frame range were checked. A separate file audit compared the source mesh and rigged duplicate. The topology values above were recorded during the earlier mesh review. These checks establish a defined input and output; they are not a general mesh-quality certificate.

B. Programmatic skeleton generation

The final armature, Hand_Rig_Reconstructed, contains 22 bones: one non-deforming Hand_Root plus 21 deform bones. The hierarchy begins Hand_Root → Hand_Wrist → Hand_Palm. The palm parents the thumb and four digit chains. The thumb has metacarpal, proximal and distal segments. Index, middle, ring and pinky each have metacarpal, proximal, middle and distal bones.

Joint positions were placed against the corrected hand geometry using measured mesh sections and proportions. Some finger joint positions used clear cross-section waists; where a waist was not distinct, proportion-based fallback placement was used. This is a documented construction strategy for this particular mesh, not a validated automatic joint-detection algorithm for arbitrary hands. The saved hierarchy and parenting were checked after reopen. Bone roll and local-axis consistency have not been accepted as anatomically correct, as the reverse-bending defect demonstrates.

The rig has no IK constraints or animator-facing control layer in the verified file. The 21 deform bones provide separate pose channels; this is skeletal articulation, not a polished control rig with sliders, limits, custom widgets or production controls.

C. Automated skinning

The rigged copy is connected to the new armature by an Armature modifier. Each deform bone has a corresponding vertex group. Native Blender automatic weights produced nonzero assignments on all 9,584 vertices. The full-file audit counted 21,379 assignments, at most four influences per vertex, and a maximum weight-sum error of 4.47 × 10⁻⁸. The sampled skin page also showed normalized per-vertex sums within floating-point precision.

The successful operation was Blender’s native automatic parent-with-weights operation, invoked on a recoverable working copy with keep-transform behavior. A later validation pass limited influences to four and normalized weights; the final saved audit confirms that bound. This does not mean the weights were manually painted or aesthetically approved. Weight coverage, influence count and normalization are structural checks. Wrist collapse, pinching, volume loss and visual smoothness still require pose review.

ForgeMCP’s typed skin-binding preview was blocked by its configured attribute-count bound. The final success therefore demonstrates a native Blender weighting route in a ForgeMCP-supported workflow, not successful completion through that specific typed binder.

D. Skeletal deformation and independent movement

The file audit posed each digit’s chain separately and compared the target region with the other four digit regions. Target-region mean displacement was approximately 0.0683 m for index, 0.0737 m for middle, 0.0660 m for ring, 0.0373 m for pinky and 0.1698 m for the thumb. Mean movement measured in non-target digit regions stayed at or near zero in those tests. The thumb also showed a separate sampled movement toward the palm region.

These are geometry-displacement results. They verify that individual pose chains affect the intended mesh region and provide evidence against broad cross-finger influence in those tested poses. They do not establish that the rotation sign is anatomically correct, that a joint rotates about the right axis, or that the silhouette looks natural. The user’s observed reversed flexion remains authoritative for that visual acceptance question and is recorded as an unresolved defect.

E. Procedural animation

The armature carries the Action Hand_Demo_Animation. It spans frames 1–120 at 24 fps, with 57 pose-bone Euler-rotation curves and 855 BEZIER keyframe points. The file audit verified the neutral pose at frame 120 against the rest geometry with a zero reported return delta. The user confirmed seeing the animation play in Blender. The record does not claim a long-duration playback soak, all-frame inspection, or approved motion quality.

The action contains independent digit poses and a partial-curl sequence. It is not accepted as a convincing closed fist. A geometric test can report motion toward a derived palm vector while a human view still reveals backward bending; that disagreement means the test’s “toward palm” criterion is not sufficient as an anatomical oracle. The next correction must define the palm-facing direction from a clearly labeled rest pose and verify motion in visual views.

F. Integrated workflow and source boundary

The observed MCP tools used for current readback were forge_list_sessions, blender_scene_info, blender_inspect_object, blender_inspect_rig, blender_inspect_skin and blender_inspect_animation. The session was selected explicitly before object-specific inspection. Scene, rig, skin and animation reads were non-mutating.

The successful native weight and animation construction used Blender Python operations in a separate Blender process on a saved working copy, followed by an independent file reopen audit. Exact durable traceability from every armature-construction and keyframe-generation statement to a committed ForgeMCP source function is incomplete. The repository contains Blender rigging, skinning, typed recipe and dispatch modules, but this individual asset result does not prove that those modules implement generalized autonomous character rigging. The documented implementation boundary is therefore: ForgeMCP connected and supplied structured inspection/orchestration and readback; native Blender operations completed the final automatic weighting and keyed deformation workflow; a saved file was reopened and measured.

Defect and corrective investigation

The dedicated issue is Incorrect finger flexion direction. Possible causes remain hypotheses: reversed rotation signs, inconsistent bone roll, incorrect local flexion axes, rest-pose mismatches, hierarchy interactions, or an inaccurate definition of the palm-facing direction. The proposed investigation captures neutral bone matrices and landmarks, rotates one joint at a time, compares fingertip trajectories in orthographic views, and tests parent/child channels independently. The correction milestone is deliberately separate; this documentation task did not alter the rig.

Acceptance requires that fingers flex toward the palm and extend back to neutral; joints use appropriate axes; fingertip paths are plausible; neighboring digits stay within defined isolation tolerances; the mesh remains stable; playback is repeatable; and the original rest pose remains recoverable. Passing weight and keyframe tests cannot close this issue.

Reusable technical validation suite

Future rigging work should report each gate as PASS, FAIL or NOT VERIFIED and preserve its evidence boundary.

  1. Construction: verify unique bone names, expected counts, valid parent references, acyclic parenting, connected flags, and bone head/tail positions inside the measured mesh bounds.
  2. Orientation: calculate bone roll and local axes against explicit anatomical vectors. Test positive and negative single-joint rotations against a documented palm-forward vector. Do not infer flexion sign from a convenient world axis.
  3. Binding: require one intended Armature modifier, the expected armature object, groups for all deform bones, and no stale group or modifier references.
  4. Weights: measure all-vertex coverage, nonzero weight count, per-vertex normalization, maximum influence count, unexpected groups, cross-digit spill and weight discontinuities across joint regions.
  5. Deformation: pose each joint and each digit independently. Record vertex and landmark displacement, target-region response, neighboring-region response, pinch, volume loss and unexpected palm/wrist motion.
  6. Intersections: evaluate the mesh over representative frames, inspect self-contact and nonadjacent surface intersections, and separate intended contact from penetration. A pair-count check is only a diagnostic; it is not a visual quality verdict.
  7. Animation: verify named Actions, expected frame range and fps, required F-curves, keyframe counts, interpolation, repeatable evaluation, and restoration of a reference neutral pose.
  8. Visual acceptance: review front, back, side and palm views at neutral, single-finger flexion, thumb opposition, partial curl and maximum intended range. Human review is mandatory because numerical tests can pass while the hand bends backward.
  9. Persistence and export: save a new version, close or independently open that exact file, read back the same mesh/rig/action, then separately test target-engine import and playback.

The evidence gates are independent. Technical functionality means the bones, weights and channels operate. Anatomical correctness means the direction and joint paths correspond to a hand. Visual quality means the deformation is acceptable at the intended camera distances and poses. Game-engine readiness requires a successful round trip in the chosen engine and verification of skeleton, materials, animation and deformation. Only the first category has substantial tool evidence in this prototype.

Reproducibility and workflow

The measured environment was Blender 5.2.3 LTS with ForgeMCP Blender adapter 0.2.49-alpha.1. Preserve the original .blend and make a versioned recovery copy before rigging. Record exact file identity, Blender version, active scene, mesh name, object transforms, topology counts, UV/material names and existing armatures before any edit. Keep the source mesh intact and build the rigged result as a new mesh object or in a new file.

For this result, the hand geometry and axis were inspected; a hand-only parent hierarchy was constructed around wrist, palm and digit segments; and a separate rigged mesh copy was bound to the armature. Native Blender automatic weights were generated using the armature automatic-parent operation with transforms preserved. The groups and modifier target were checked, influences limited to four, and weights normalized. Pose-bone rotation channels were keyed into Hand_Demo_Animation. The file was saved under a new version name, then reopened independently and checked for counts, parentage, geometry equivalence, UV/material retention, weight sums, motion isolation, Action metadata and neutral restoration.

A developer repeating this path must treat the exact bone coordinates and sign tests as mesh-specific. The source’s non-manifold/boundary findings must be reviewed before relying on deformation or export. If a typed ForgeMCP operation rejects a payload, record the code and bound, do not replay it blindly, and select an explicitly documented native fallback only on a disposable copy. Auto-Rig Pro is not a required component of the final v002 method; this artifact is a custom hand rig, not an ARP-generated skeleton. The exact input mesh identity, all measured counts, all fallback steps, and the final output version should be attached to every reproduction.

The captured final artifact is Hand_Rig_Animation_Final_20261030_v002.blend. Its independent saved-file verification and current live ForgeMCP readback are evidence for this one file. They do not validate an unobserved copy, another mesh, another Blender version or another rigging path.

Development significance and roadmap

The milestone links scene understanding to a persistent, deforming, animated asset. That is useful for ForgeMCP because character work depends on coordinated state: a bone must belong to the intended skeleton, a group must address the right deform bone, the modifier must target that armature, animation curves must reference valid pose channels, and saved output must reopen. Demonstrating these relationships together gives a more meaningful integration test than reporting that a single bone or keyframe was created.

For game development, a reusable hand workflow could support interaction poses, first-person animation, procedural gestures, equipment handling and retargeted motion. For AI-assisted authoring, it offers a future sequence in which an agent inspects geometry, proposes a rig, previews a deformation, receives visual review, and records a validated result. For Genesis Engine, a hand asset could eventually exercise skeletal import, pose playback, and animation interfaces once the Blender output passes anatomical and engine-side checks.

Those are architectural opportunities, not current product capabilities. Reusable templates still need explicit hand proportions and coordinate conventions. Automated joint placement needs diverse mesh fixtures and confidence reporting. Weight correction needs stress-pose metrics and visual review. Retargeting needs a mapping between source and destination skeletons. Game-engine verification needs import/export receipts and runtime pose comparisons. None is established by this milestone.

The next engineering milestone is Anatomical Rig Validation & Automated Deformation Correction. A separate future proposal, Real-Time Hand Motion Capture and Skeletal Retargeting, outlines local webcam tracking; it is not implemented here.

Final disposition

The evidence supports a successful functional prototype: a hand-only skeleton, automatic skin weights, individually responsive digits, a keyed action, and a saved file read back in Blender. The evidence does not support “production-ready,” “anatomically correct,” “fully autonomous arbitrary rigging,” “Auto-Rig Pro-generated,” or “game-engine ready.” Reverse finger flexion is the accepted open defect and the next work item. Webcam tracking remains a proposal only.
